content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
First off, the title needs changing as it doesn't make much grammatical sense! "Revisiting" instead of "Revisit" would be much better. The paper is well written, so I'm surprised the title isn't :)

In this work, the authors examine the effects of using knowledge distillation in two unusual scenarios. Firstly, when the student network is fully-trained but is weaker than the teacher, and secondly, when the teacher network is only partially trained. In both cases, the student benefits, implying that "dark knowledge" between class labels is a nonsense, and all it's really doing is label smoothing.

I must admit, I really like these experiments, and I'm broadly a fan of this paper. I do have a few comments.

It's important to note that the Hinton et al. paper builds heavily on an earlier work (https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6184v5), which I would recommend citing. Also, I don't like the use of "surprising" in the prose, but that's just down to taste.

Section 2 is good, but it don't understand why there is a separate list of student networks and teacher networks. Why not just put every combination of them? Error bars are good. For Table 1 why does ResNetXt get ResNet18 as a student when the other networks didn't?

Table 10 in the appendix is concerning. I don't see why there are different temperatures and alphas in use. At least with temperature, there is only one case where it isn't set to 20 (why is it 6 for ResNeXt29-ResNet18?). Why does alpha differ so heavily across experiments? This creates the (hopefully unintended) image that your results have been cherry picked. I would strongly recommend either using the same alpha/temp for each experiment, or providing a strong justification why it differs between networks.

The comparison between label smoothing and KD is neat.

The first method suggested (Tf-KDself) is *exactly* what the authors use in Born-again nets (https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04770). I notice that this paper has been cited briefly in the small related work section at the end, but this really should feature earlier as it's not a great look to pass off an older method as something new (although this may be unintentional).

The difference between the virtual teacher approach and LSR is so subtle that I'm surprised there is much difference in results. The only comparison that I can find is the table in Figure 6 but this is missing error bars (I am using error bars and STDs interchangeably). I would like to see a comparison with error bars (although this could be on say, CIFAR-100 if ImageNet is too expensive).

On a related note, the table in Figure 4 could benefit form error bars.

Pros:
- Experiments in Section 2 are novel and interesting, as far as I am aware
- Experiments are conducted across different datasets and networks, suggesting generalisation
- Paper is well written (apart from the title. Please change!)

Cons:
- The use of different hyperparameters across experiments is concerning
- Tf-KDself is just a rebranding of Born-Again-Neural networks
- It is not clear how/why the virtual teacher surpasses label smoothing

I propose the paper should receive a weak accept. It is well written (but please change the title), interesting, and experimentally satisfying. However, I would caveat this by strongly recommending that the authors address my concerns regarding hyperparameter changes. It would be a real shame if this was a case of cherry-picking experiments to suit a hypothesis.

display_title: Thank you for the supportive review!

content.title: Thank you for the supportive review!
content.comment:
First of all, we already changed the title as “Revisiting Knowledge distillation: a Teacher-free Framework” in the revision (Thanks again!).  And for the changes of hyper-parameters, we do not pick hyper-parameters but search all hyper-parameters with 70 epochs training (200 epochs in total) on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny-ImageNet. Eight GPUs (4 NVIDIA TITAN X and 4 NVIDIA TITAN V) were used for grid search. We don’t search the hyper-parameters on ImageNet because of expensive computational costs. We already released our codes, in which you can run “python search_hyperparameters.py” to check our grid-search process on CIFAR100. 

Then the followings are point-to-point responses to your comments:
Q1. the Hinton et al. paper builds heavily on an earlier work (https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6184v5), which I would recommend citing. Also, I don't like the use of "surprising" in the prose, but that's just down to taste.
A1. We already add the citation of the original paper and delete “surprising” in this revision.

Q2. “Section 2 is good, but it don't understand why there is a separate list of student networks and teacher networks. … For Table 1 why does ResNetXt get ResNet18 as a student when the other networks didn't? ”
A2. We agree with you that combinations format between all student and teacher networks are better than a separate list, but we do not find a good format to present the tables in Section 2 which can show our results clearly and also save the space simultaneously. If you have format as a recommendation, we are happy to consider to use it. For ResNetXt (Teacher) and ResNet18 (Student) in Table1, we just want to show that for a stronger student model ResNet18 (compared with student models: MobileNet and ShuffleNet), the counterintuitive results Re-KD still exist (student can improve teacher). We should explain it clearly in paper. 

Q3. Table 10 in the appendix is concerning. I don't see why there are different temperatures and alphas in use. 
A3. We searched the hyper-parameters rather than picked. So the temperatures and alphas are different for different models.

Q4. Tf-KD_self and Born-again nets.
A4. We agree with you that Tf-KD_self is very similar to Born-again nets. The difference is that Born-again nets utilize an ensemble of student model as a teacher in the final step. The exploratory experiments and the relationship between KD and LSR also can explain why Born-again nets works. We already add some clarification about the relationships between Tf-KD_self and Born-again nets in Related Work.

Q5. The difference between the virtual teacher approach and LSR is so subtle that I'm surprised there is much difference in results.
A5. Please refer to A3 to Reviewer #3.

Q6. Missing error bars in the table of Figure 4 and Figure6.
A6. We already add standard deviations for the table of Figure4 (CIFAR100) in this revision. But it is computation expensive for ImageNet (table in figure 6). 

I hope our answers can address your concerns. Thanks!

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This submission takes a critical look at knowledge distillation (KD) and asks the important question whether or not it’s just plain regularization in disguise. It shows some interesting evidence to support this and suggests simpler KD variants based on this insight.

I think it’s a great premise, but I will have to land on Weak Reject because of weaknesses in the suggested Tf-KD versions. I think the Tf_KD_reg is just label smoothing, which removes the primary novelty of the paper. I think this is a grave error, but I do not go below a weak reject since I do like the premise and the observations in the first half and think they hold some merit on their own.

Premise:  

The premise of the paper to link KD with LSR and the experiments showing evidence that unintuitive or even poor KD can be effective are great. I think it’s a great starting point and I would like to see more in this direction. I am not surprised by this conclusion either, so it is important to point out.

Experimental thoroughness:

There are plenty of experiments, many models and datasets, with repeated runs and error bars. High marks for this. However, as I will point out shortly, I don’t think the hyper-parameters were necessarily chosen carefully.

Tf-KD_reg:

The main contribution is Tf-KD_reg, so let's take a closer look. Using an “almost correct” teacher looks identical to label smoothing to me. I provide some mathematical arguments that this is true.

Eq. (2) establishes what you get if you blend two distributions. Let’s denote this q’_alpha, since we may want to change the mixing ratio alpha. So, if we define u here as another version of Eq. (1), but taking q’_beta, the results will be exactly q’_{alpha*beta}. What this shows is that if we do an alpha-convex blend with q’_beta, then it’s equivalent to doing a alpha*beta-convex blend with the uniform distribution. With this established, note that Eq. (8) can be written as q’_{(1 - a)*K/(K-1)}. So, when that is plugged in, it simply turns into blending directly with a uniform distribution (i.e. label smoothing) with mixing ratio alpha*(1-a)*K/(K-1). Label smoothing has one parameter alpha, while this teacher-free formulation has alpha and “a” - it’s simply an over-parameterized version of label smoothing. Adding temperature “tau” to the mix is even further over-parameterization. The fact that LSR does worse probably just means that the tables are a comparison between two different smoothing strengths of LSR - one which is better. Try changing the alpha in LSR with a factor (1-a)*K/(K-1) and see if you now get the same results. Please let me know if there is a difference I’m failing to see. I may have rushed the derivations, but I think it's intuitively clear that they are at least very similar, if not identical.

Tf-KD_self:

I disagree that we should call this “teacher free”, since it does have a teacher that needs to be pre-trained prior to training the student. The only novelty is that the student and the teacher share the same network. This is a very modest novelty, but I agree it has some benefits, especially when integrating this technique into a deep learning framework, where it would be as easy as a flip of a switch.

display_title: Thanks a lot for your valuable comments!

content.title: Thanks a lot for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
First of all, Tf-KD_reg is not label smoothing, your derivations between label smoothing and Tf-KD_reg is correct when temperature \tau=1, but wrong when \tau is not 1. Please refer to A3 for details. The followings are the point-to-point response. 

Q1. Premise.
A1. Thank you for admiring that we link KD with LSR and the experiment part of poorly-trained KD. We still believe the Teacher-free part also very important in our paper.

Q2. Experimental thoroughness.
A2. The hyper-parameters on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet are obtained by grid-search with 70 epochs training (200 epochs in total).  We used eight GPUs (four NVIDIA TITAN X, four NVIDIA TITAN V) to search hyper-parameters for dataset CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny-ImageNet in our paper. We don’t search the hyper-parameters on ImageNet because of computational costs and adopt the most common parameters for our methods (in most of cases: \tau=20, \alpha=0.1, a=0.99) and LSR (\alpha=0.1). We already released the codes, in which you can try “python search_hyperparameters.py” to check our grid-search process on CIFAR100. 
 
Q3. Tf-KD_reg:  (a). “the main contribution is Tf-KD_reg. ”
                            (b). “Tf-KD_reg looked identical to label smoothing to me. ”
A3.  (a) Tf-KD_reg is one of our contributions, we also claimed that the Reversed KD and Poorly-trained KD also are our main contributions.  
A3.  (b) Your derivations are correct when temperature “\tau=1”, but it is wrong when "\tau is not 1". Because you do not consider that the output of the student also is softened by temperature \tau, you cannot directly mix the two terms in Tf-KD_reg as Eq.(2) when \tau is not 1.  In the normal case of KD and Tf-KD, we do not make \tau=1. And if we let alpha in LSR with a factor (1-a)*K/(K-1), the results of LSR are different from Tf-KD_reg, and the accuracy of LSR will become worse. We conduct experiments to validate your idea on CIFAR100 by using MobileNetV2, ShuffleNetV2 and ResNet18, the results are the following:
======================================================================================
Model                     Baseline         LSR (\alpha=0.1)          LSR (\alpha*(1-a)*K/(K-1))            Tf-KD_reg
MobileNetV2             68.38           69.32±0.28 (+0.94)               68.59±0.35 (+0.21)              70.88±0.27 (+2.50) 
ShuffleNetV2             70.34           70.83±0.19 (+0.49)               70.53±0.21 (+0.19）           72.09±0.31 (+1.75)
ResNet18                   75.87            77.28±0.23 (+1.39)              76.05±0.13 (+0.18)              77.36±0.24 (+1.49)
=======================================================================================
On CIFAR100, we set a=0.99 in our paper and K=100, so \alpha'=\alpha*(1-a)*K/(K-1)=0.1*0.01*100/99=1.01e-4, which is a small value.  As you can see,  the accuracy from your derivations become worse than \alpha=0.1, of course, much worse than Tf-KD_reg.  We also searched \alpha for label smoothing and found that in most of the cases label smoothing gets the best result when \alpha is around 0.1.  Based on these analyses and experiments, we do not take Tf-KD_reg as an over-parameterized version of label smoothing.
You can check our results by running label smoothing experiments as:
python main.py --model_dir experiments/base_experiments/base_mobilenetv2/ --label_smoothing –-alpha 0.000101
python main.py --model_dir experiments/base_experiments/base_resnet18/ --label_smoothing –alpha 0.000101

Additionally, we stated in our paper that the original KD is also very similar to LSR, which can be seen as a learned type of LSR. So it is normal that Tf-KD_reg has a similar format with LSR, but they are different. We sincerely hope you can change your comments if you think we are right! 

Q4. Tf-KD_self: "I disagree that we should call this “teacher free” since it does have a teacher that needs to be pre-trained prior to training the student."
A4. In common belief, the teacher in KD is a stronger model with more parameters or higher learning capacity. We consider Tf-KD_self as one of the teacher-free methods because the model self is not a model with more parameters or stronger learning capacity.  But we also agree with you to some degree because in such a case the teacher is itself. Besides, Tf-KD_{self} is simple but effective, and you also agree that it has benefits, especially when integrating this technique into a deep learning framework.


We hope our answers can address your concerns. I am looking forward to your reply for our responses!

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper connects knowledge distillation and label smoothing regularization. With two sets of well designed experiments, train large network with small teacher or poorly trained teacher, the authors claim knowledge distillation has a strong regularization effect. The authors then show that both knowledge distillation and label smoothing loss can be written as linear combination of supervised learning loss and KL divergence loss. Finally, two “teacher free” methods are proposed, use the same network as student and teacher, and a variant of label smoothing.  

I am generally on the fence for this paper. I think it makes sense to view knowledge distillation as a regularizer. It is not a surprising finding but I have not seen it in previous papers. On the other hand, there are multiple ways to interpret knowledge distillation, including categorical relationship, loss smoothing, and regularizer. It is hard to convince me regularization is the main drive because in original KD, even without the supervised part H(q, p), it still works reasonably well. It looks to me this paper is more about label smoothing/regularization than knowledge distillation. But since label smoothing has been shown to be an effective regularizer in previous works, it is difficult to say how much practical value is there. 

About the two proposed teacher free methods, the first one looks like Born Again Network, the second looks like can be achieved by tuning the label smoothing parameter \alpha. 

A relatively minor issue is how the hyper-parameters (\alpha and there should be a temperature parameter T) are decided for knowledge distillation.

display_title: Thanks a lot for your valuable comments!

content.title: Thanks a lot for your valuable comments!
content.comment:
Q1. It is not a surprising finding but I have not seen it in previous papers.
A1. The counterintuitive results of Reverse-KD and Defective KD are found by our work for the first time. We believe such results can motivate us to rethink knowledge distillation. As supported by the other two reviewers, the two exploration experiments (Reverse-KD and Defective KD) are the most interesting part of the paper.

Q2.(a) There are multiple ways to interpret knowledge distillation, including categorical relationship, loss smoothing, and regularizer. (b) It is hard to convince me regularization is the main drive because in original KD, even without the supervised part H(q, p), it still works reasonably well. 
A2.(a) Yes, we agree with you that there are multiple ways to interpret knowledge distillation.  And our work does not deny the importance of categorical information, because a high-accuracy teacher can still improve a student better than the low-accuracy teacher because of more accurate categorical information (Figure2 in our paper). But the gap between student model and teacher model is large when the teacher model is too stronger[1], this phenomenon also indicates that the categorical information cannot work as good as we expect. So until now, we cannot explain KD by just one theory, and categorical relationship, loss smoothing, and regularization are potential directions.  Our work explains KD by using regularization, which is based on the experimental observation, especially from the results of the Defective-KD experiment (Section 2). The results of exploratory experiments can be explained by the regularization, i.e. the relationships between KD and LSR. 
A2.(b) Without the supervised part H(q, p), the student can still be trained reasonably well (we did experiments to validate it, not given in our paper). But at the same time, without categorical information from the teacher, we can find the student can still be trained very well by only adding a regularization term, reaching the performance taught by a superior teacher. So the regularization can play an important role as a superior teacher. We also did extra experiments to validate such improvement is not contributed by simply tuning the hyper-parameters of label smoothing (please refer to the A3 to Reviewer#3 for details).

Q3. About the two proposed teacher free methods, the first one looks like Born Again Network, the second looks like can be achieved by tuning the label smoothing parameter \alpha.
A3. The first method Tf-KD_self is similar to Born Again Network[1], the difference is that the paper of Born Again Network uses an ensemble of students to train itself as the final step. We added clarification in our revision (Related Work). Thank you for point this! For our second method Tf-KD_reg, it is not achieved by tuning the label smoothing parameter \alpha. Reviewer#3 also has similar comments, please refer to the A3 to Reviewer#3 for details.
      
Q4. A relatively minor issue is how the hyper-parameters (\alpha and there should be a temperature parameter \tau) are decided for knowledge distillation. 
A4. We use grid-search to find the best hyper-parameters for CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny-ImageNet, not for ImageNet because of computation cost. Due to the huge number of experiments, we just search 70 epochs (total 200 epochs) to find the best hyper-parameters.  We already released our codes, in which you can run “python search_hyperparameters.py” to check our grid-search process on CIFAR100. 


We hope our answers can address your concerns. 

[1] Mirzadeh, Seyed-Iman, et al. "Improved knowledge distillation via teacher assistant: Bridging the gap between student and teacher." arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.03393 (2019).

replying_to: Replying to Thanks a lot for your valuable comments!

content.title: Regarding Q2
content.comment:
Hi authors,

I agree with the reviewer that even without the hard label, KD can work well, which has been empirically verified in [1]. Also, in my experience, $\tau$ doesn't have to be 1 for it to work well. Judging from [1], I do not think when $\tau=1$ the soft-label is similar to the hard-label (at least on large-scale dataset like ImageNet). Lastly, I'd like to point out that the performance is "better" than normal training but not worse [1].

[1] Bagherinezhad, Hessam, et al. "Label refinery: Improving imagenet classification through label progression." ECCV (2018).
